text.p: Base metal trading on the LME remained fairly humdrum during Tuesday afternoon, and although prices moved up from early lows there was little substance in movements.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index rose 1.52 points to 245.49.

LME copper traders said copper led the way, but again lost impetus at the $2,380 level, while nickel fluctuated wildly, but was always in the minus column, due to rising inventories and less concern over Russian supply disruption. LME prices made little real headway, with prices some way off the upper and lower ends of the current range. Consequently, volume was thin. There was more interest this afternoon, but stops were not hit above $2,380, and last kerb trade was at $2,377, up $10 a tonne from Monday.

Nickel trading was volatile, with the market showing its usual unpredictability in the face of fundamental developments, although the trend was generally lower. Losses were initially induced by the 846-tonne increase in stocks before the market perversely rallied away from lows under $7,700, despite news that Norilsk workers had decided not to halt output.

Aluminium turned away from its lows during the afternoon, but remained softer following a morning sell-off. Traders said the rally back above $1,650 lacked conviction, and final business was at $1,653, down $4.

Zinc also reversed direction during the afternoon, with price dips seen as buying opportunities at present, while another inventory trend was also indicative of solid fundamentals. Interest picked up during the kerb, when there was another foray above $1,300, although three months ended at $1,299, up $5 from the previous close
Lead recovered from a midsession sell-off by Chinese operators, but the pace of trading was slow, matching dull physicals, and by the end of the kerb prices were still unchanged at $679 a tonne.

Tin sentiment took a knock from the 700-tonne rise in stocks, which followed a sizeable increase last Friday. The short-lived backwardation of last week has attracted some 1,100 tonnes of metal to the market, with total stocks now at 10,205 tonnes. Prices held above the lows during late trading, helped by copper's snap up, but last kerb trade at $5,845 was still down $25.
Alloy was quiet, but closed at a stable $1,545/55 a tonne.

CBOT wheat futures were higher at midsession, boosted by concerns of a deterioration in hard red winter wheat crop conditions in Texas and Oklahoma, traders said. At 1051 CST, wheat was up three to 4-3/4 cents a bushel with May up three at $3.89-1/2. New crop July was up four at $3.84-1/2.

NYMEX heating oil futures were firm in early afternoon trading Tuesday as recent cold weather helped to reverse the usual seasonal price decline, traders said. Crude futures were slightly higher, helped by unrest in one of Nigeria's oil-producing regions, but the sector was looking technically "toppy" unless there was news of a major supply disruption, taders said. April heating oil was up 0.82 cents at 56.55 cents a gallon at 1315 EST, down from a high of 57.10 cents. May crude was up three cents at $21.10 a barrel.

New York precious metals remained weaker at midday, but the selling pressure that took hold at mid-morning had eased as the market moved into a holding mode ahead of the FOMC outcome due about 1415 EST, traders said. Some traders were mystified why the selling in gold and silver came after the over-the-counter options expiry at 0930 EST. Any attempts to push down the price are usually made just before expiry in order to bring a strike price into the money, floor sources said. COMEX April gold was off $1.20 at $349.70 an ounce. Bullion was quoted at $348.70/$349.20.
